headings.140: C. Application to the Facts of This Case (1) No New Facts

blocks.overview: This case concerns the interpretation and application of section 515(10)(c) of the Criminal Code regarding pre-trial detention to maintain public confidence in the justice system. The applicant is the Crown appealing the Superior Court's order releasing the respondent, St-Cloud, charged with aggravated assault. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, restoring the detention order under s. 515(10)(c).

blocks.issue: When is pre-trial detention necessary to maintain public confidence under s. 515(10)(c) of the Criminal Code?
blocks.court_conclusion: Detention under s. 515(10)(c) is not limited to exceptional crimes; all circumstances must be balanced from a reasonable, informed public perspective.

positions.text: Courts have unduly restricted s. 515(10)(c) scope; restrictive approach must be rejected; detention justified if four factors favor it unless other circumstances justify release.
s. 515(10)(c) applies rarely; four factors must be weighted; focus on whether confidence maintained if accused released; crime explainability relevant.
Justice Lavergne and Judge Legault found detention necessary under s. 515(10)(c) based on offence gravity, prosecution strength, and public confidence.
s. 515(10)(c) is distinct ground for detention; requires balancing four factors and all circumstances; public means reasonable, informed persons; detention necessary to maintain confidence.

blocks.issue: What is the scope and nature of the review power under ss. 520 and 521 of the Criminal Code for detention decisions?
blocks.court_conclusion: Review is a hybrid remedy limited to new evidence, error of law, or clearly inappropriate decisions; no open-ended discretion or de novo hearing.

positions.text: Review should be limited to error in principle or clear unreasonableness, similar to sentencing appeals; open-ended discretion rejected.
Interim release is constitutional right distinct from sentencing; review rules should differ accordingly.
Martin J. granted release on review, finding errors in initial detention decision and restricted s. 515(10)(c) scope.
Ss. 520 and 521 do not allow de novo hearing; reviewing judge must respect initial justice's fact findings unless error or clear inappropriateness; new evidence admissible if truly new.

propositions.text: Canadians believe liberty and presumption of innocence are fundamental and must be protected
Confidence requires accused not to evade justice, harm others, or interfere while awaiting trial
Parliament recognized risk to justice system's repute in s. 515(10)(a) and (b) Cr. C. for interim detention

paragraphs.summary: The court states Canadians value liberty and presumption of innocence, but Parliament allows interim detention to protect justice system's repute.

propositions.text: Parliament added s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C. for detention to maintain confidence in justice system
Allowing accused release despite overwhelming evidence may undermine public confidence: R. v. Hall para 26

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Parliament added s. 515(10)(c) to prevent release that undermines public confidence, citing R. v. Hall.

propositions.text: This appeal considers when pre-trial detention is necessary to maintain public confidence under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.
Hall addressed constitutionality of s. 515(10)(c) but not its application
Lower courts have interpreted s. 515(10)(c) inconsistently, requiring further guidance

paragraphs.summary: The court notes this appeal addresses s. 515(10)(c)'s application due to inconsistent lower court interpretations since Hall.

propositions.text: Detention under s. 515(10)(c) requires balancing accused's rights and justice in community: Hall para 41
Judges must adopt public perspective in deciding detention necessity under s. 515(10)(c)
Meaning of 'public' is difficult, causing discussion and inconsistent results

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 515(10)(c) requires balancing rights and public perspective, but 'public' meaning causes inconsistent results.

propositions.text: Courts have unduly restricted s. 515(10)(c) scope to exceptional crimes or classes
Misunderstanding of 'public' in French and English versions truncated s. 515(10)(c) interpretation
'Public' means reasonable, well-informed community members, not legal experts

paragraphs.summary: The court argues s. 515(10)(c) scope is unduly restricted and 'public' means reasonable community members, not legal experts.

propositions.text: This is first time Court considers review power under ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. for detention decisions
Review power is limited to three situations: new evidence, error of law, or clearly inappropriate decision
Reviewing judge cannot substitute own evidence assessment but can intervene if weight given to factors is excessive or insufficient

paragraphs.summary: The court limits review power under ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. to new evidence, legal error, or clearly inappropriate decisions.

propositions.text: Respondent St-Cloud charged with aggravated assault under s. 268 Cr. C.
Justice of the peace ordered detention under s. 515(10)(b) and (c) Cr. C.
Justice at preliminary inquiry upheld detention under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.
Respondent applied for review under s. 520 Cr. C.; Superior Court judge ordered release
Crown appeals Superior Court release order to this Court

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts St-Cloud's detention orders, Superior Court release, and Crown's appeal to this Court.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed; detention necessary to maintain confidence in justice administration
Court will explain reasons for allowing appeal

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal and will explain why detention is necessary to maintain public confidence.

propositions.text: On April 24, 2013, respondent and two others violently assaulted a bus driver, recorded on video
Victim suffered serious long-term injuries; respondent charged with aggravated assault under s. 268 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the violent assault by respondent and others causing serious injuries, leading to aggravated assault charge.

propositions.text: First release hearing on April 26, 2013 before Judge Lavergne; appellant opposed release
Victim was hospitalized with uncertain prognosis including facial fracture and concussion

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the first release hearing where appellant opposed release and victim's serious medical condition.

propositions.text: Judge Lavergne stated prosecutor's onus to show detention necessity
Judge Lavergne found detention necessary under s. 515(10)(b) Cr. C. for public protection

paragraphs.summary: Judge Lavergne found detention necessary for public protection under s. 515(10)(b) Cr. C., with prosecutor bearing onus.

propositions.text: Judge Lavergne considered s. 515(10)(c) factors: prosecution strength, offence gravity, circumstances, potential sentence
Aggravating factors evident from case circumstances

paragraphs.summary: Judge Lavergne considered s. 515(10)(c) factors and found aggravating circumstances in the case.

propositions.text: s. 515(10)(c) requires analysis if reasonable collective expectation denies interim release to maintain public confidence
Public means reasonable, dispassionate, informed persons aware of presumption of innocence and crime circumstances
Videotape and circumstances justify denial of interim release to maintain public confidence

paragraphs.summary: Judge Lavergne explained s. 515(10)(c) requires reasonable public expectation to deny release, and found such expectation here.

propositions.text: Judge Lavergne ordered respondent's detention until further order under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Judge Lavergne ordered detention of respondent under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Respondent applied for release after preliminary inquiry under s. 523(2)(b) Cr. C.
Onus on respondent to show new cause for release; court has limited power requiring restraint

paragraphs.summary: Judge Legault noted respondent's onus to show new cause for release and court's limited power requiring restraint.

propositions.text: Evidence on offence circumstances unchanged; new facts include increased financial security and possible employment

paragraphs.summary: Judge Legault found some new facts like increased financial security and possible employment despite unchanged offence evidence.

propositions.text: Risk of reoffending reduced; respondent credible in commitment to work or study
Victim's medical condition worsened

paragraphs.summary: Judge Legault found reduced reoffending risk and worsening victim condition.

propositions.text: Judge Legault accepted detention necessary to maintain confidence under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.
Reasonable collective expectation exists to deny interim release to maintain public confidence

paragraphs.summary: Judge Legault upheld detention under s. 515(10)(c) due to reasonable public expectation to deny release.

propositions.text: Respondent applied to Superior Court under s. 520 Cr. C. for review of detention order on July 2, 2013

paragraphs.summary: Respondent applied for Superior Court review of detention order under s. 520 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Martin J. understood Judge Legault found detention unnecessary under s. 515(10)(b) Cr. C.
Martin J. noted Judge Legault would have granted bail but for s. 515(10)(c) ground

paragraphs.summary: Martin J. noted Judge Legault would grant bail absent s. 515(10)(c) ground for detention.

propositions.text: Martin J. noted respondent must show reviewable error by justices ordering detention
Section 515(10)(c) Cr. C. must be used sparingly, per Hall

paragraphs.summary: Martin J. noted respondent must show reviewable error and that s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C. must be used sparingly, citing Hall.

propositions.text: Test: whether a reasonable, disinterested person versed in Charter and law would see release as undermining confidence in justice
Justice must assess this test based on facts in evidence

paragraphs.summary: Martin J. stated the test for bail denial involves an objective reasonable person assessing confidence in justice, based on evidence.

propositions.text: Incident was repugnant, heinous, unjustifiable but explainable
Two justices erred in denying release under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.
Respondent's application granted and release ordered

paragraphs.summary: Martin J. found the incident heinous but explainable, that justices erred denying release, and ordered respondent's release.

propositions.text: This appeal raises the following questions

paragraphs.summary: The appeal raises specific questions to be addressed.

propositions.text: Legislative history of s. 515(10) Cr. C. was explained in Hall but will be summarized here

paragraphs.summary: The court will summarize the legislative history of s. 515(10) Cr. C. despite Hall's explanation.

propositions.text: Pre-trial release provisions date back to 1869 legislation making bail discretionary
Bail was discretionary with judges considering offence nature, penalty, evidence, and accused's character
1972 Bail Reform Act identified two branches for refusing bail: attendance assurance and public interest/safety
Use of 'or' led to view of three grounds for denying bail: attendance, protection, public interest
These grounds were originally s. 457(7)(a) and (b) and later s. 515(10)(a) and (b)

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines bail law history from 1869 to 1972, describing grounds for denying bail and statutory evolution.

propositions.text: Since 1982 Charter s. 11(e) guarantees right not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause
R. v. Pearson states s. 11(e) creates entitlement to reasonable bail unless just cause shown
Section 11(e) has two components: right to reasonable bail quantum and right not to be denied bail without just cause

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Charter s. 11(e) guarantees reasonable bail unless just cause, citing Pearson and defining components.

propositions.text: R. v. Morales struck down s. 515(10)(b) ground of 'public interest' as vague and authorizing standardless detention

paragraphs.summary: R. v. Morales found s. 515(10)(b) 'public interest' ground vague and unconstitutional for standardless detention.

propositions.text: In 1997 Parliament amended s. 515(10) and added para. (c) allowing detention to maintain confidence in justice
At that time, no list of circumstances was specified for justices to consider under para. (c)

paragraphs.summary: Parliament amended s. 515(10) in 1997 adding para. (c) for detention to maintain confidence, without specifying factors.

propositions.text: Hall held first part of s. 515(10)(c) authorizing denial for 'any other just cause' unconstitutional
Broad discretion to deny bail without specified basis violates presumption of innocence and s. 11(e)
Remaining part of s. 515(10)(c) found constitutional

paragraphs.summary: Hall found 'any other just cause' in s. 515(10)(c) unconstitutional but upheld remainder of provision.

propositions.text: In 2008 Parliament amended s. 515(10)(c) to align with Hall decision
Current s. 515(10)(c) includes four factors for detention to maintain confidence in justice
This version is at issue in this appeal

paragraphs.summary: The 2008 amendment to s. 515(10)(c) includes four factors and is the provision under appeal.

propositions.text: Central issue in Hall was constitutionality of s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.
Hall provided guidance on interpreting s. 515(10)(c)

paragraphs.summary: Hall's central issue was s. 515(10)(c) constitutionality and it provided interpretive guidance.

propositions.text: McLachlin C.J. explained bail denial may be necessary to maintain public confidence even without risk of absconding or reoffending
Public confidence is essential to bail and justice system functioning
Citing Valente v. The Queen on importance of public confidence

paragraphs.summary: McLachlin C.J. stated bail denial may be needed to maintain public confidence, essential to justice system, citing Valente.

propositions.text: Section 515(10)(c) is a distinct ground for detention, not residual or catch-all
Same facts may be relevant to all grounds but distinctiveness remains

paragraphs.summary: Section 515(10)(c) is a distinct bail denial ground, not residual, even if facts overlap with other grounds.

propositions.text: Justice must consider four factors specified by Parliament under s. 515(10)(c) to deny bail
Judge must appraise objectively whether reasonable community member would see denial as necessary to maintain confidence
Provision does not authorize standardless discretion but balances accused's rights and community justice needs

paragraphs.summary: Hall requires objective appraisal of four factors to deny bail under s. 515(10)(c), balancing rights and justice confidence.

propositions.text: Court will revisit Hall and consider additional passages later

paragraphs.summary: Court will further analyze Hall's passages later.

propositions.text: Appellant submits courts have artificially added factors to s. 515(10)(c) to restrict its scope
Such restrictive approach must be rejected

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues courts wrongly added factors to restrict s. 515(10)(c) scope and this must be rejected.

propositions.text: Respondent submits s. 515(10)(c) applies rarely and four factors must be weighted
Justice must focus on whether confidence in justice would be maintained if accused released

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues s. 515(10)(c) applies rarely, factors weighted, focusing on maintaining confidence if accused released.

propositions.text: Some decisions apply s. 515(10)(c) strictly and sparingly
Appellate courts have stated s. 515(10)(c) justified only in rare or exceptional circumstances
Some courts require 'something more' beyond four factors for s. 515(10)(c) application
Ontario Court of Appeal views 'something more' as conveying need to use s. 515(10)(c) sparingly
Third ground not limited to most heinous offences and can apply without community horror or fear

paragraphs.summary: Court notes some courts apply s. 515(10)(c) sparingly, require 'something more', but it can apply beyond heinous offences.

propositions.text: Two reasons—legislation and case law—explain why appellate courts interpret s. 515(10)(c) restrictively

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies legislative and case law reasons for restrictive appellate interpretations of s. 515(10)(c).

propositions.text: Former s. 515(10) Cr. C. specified two grounds for pre-trial detention: primary and secondary.
Primary ground in s. 515(10)(a) was to ensure accused's attendance in court.
Secondary ground in s. 515(10)(b) was detention necessary in public interest or for public protection.
Accused could be detained on secondary ground only if primary ground was not justified.
Secondary ground's 'public interest' component was struck down in Morales.
Since 1997 wording change, s. 515(10) no longer provides hierarchy of grounds for detention.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains former s. 515(10) Cr. C. had primary and secondary grounds for detention; secondary ground's public interest part was struck down in Morales; hierarchy removed in 1997.

propositions.text: Certain courts misinterpret Hall by preferring minority reasons over Chief Justice's majority reasons.
Minority judges in Hall would have struck down s. 515(10)(c) entirely, seeing factors as a 'facade of precision'.
Minority viewed 'maintain confidence in administration of justice' as reviving struck down 'public interest' ground.
Some courts use minority reasons to find majority advocated restrictive interpretation of s. 515(10)(c).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds some courts misinterpret Hall by favoring minority reasons that would strike down s. 515(10)(c) and see 'maintain confidence' as vague.

propositions.text: Crime in Hall was heinous murder with 37 slash wounds and intent to decapitate.
Murder caused significant public concern.
Accused's bail was denied under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker describes heinous murder and bail denial under s. 515(10)(c) in Hall.

propositions.text: Hall described crime as 'heinous and unexplained'.
Quoted R. v. Rondeau that unexplained crimes increase bail concerns for society.
Rondeau concerned secondary ground for detention, not s. 515(10)(c) which was not yet in force.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Hall described crime as heinous and unexplained, quoting Rondeau on bail concerns; Rondeau predates s. 515(10)(c).

propositions.text: Hall stated horrific, inexplicable crimes linked to accused risk public confidence in justice system.

paragraphs.summary: Court reproduces Hall's statement that horrific crimes linked to accused risk public confidence in justice.

propositions.text: Some courts misinterpret Hall by ignoring case context and specific horrific crime circumstances.
Court's description of crime as horrific was factual observation, not a prerequisite for s. 515(10)(c).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds some courts misinterpret Hall by treating horrific crime description as prerequisite rather than factual observation.

propositions.text: Whether a crime is 'unexplainable' or 'unexplained' is not a criterion under s. 515(10)(c).
Concept of 'unexplainable' crime is ambiguous and confusing.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds 'unexplainable' crime is not a criterion under s. 515(10)(c) and is ambiguous and confusing.

propositions.text: Many crimes may be explainable by provocation, mental illness, or intoxication, limiting usefulness of 'unexplainable' criterion.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds many crimes may be explainable, so 'unexplainable' crime criterion is of little assistance.

propositions.text: Applying 'unexplainable' crime criterion could exclude heinous crimes and imply justifying some crimes.
Hall's decision was based on brutal nature, strong evidence, and community fear, not 'unexplainable' crime.
Case law drift shows need to limit use of 'unexplainable' crime criterion to avoid public misperception.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds 'unexplainable' crime criterion could exclude heinous crimes and mislead public; Hall based decision on brutality, evidence, and fear.

propositions.text: Detention may be justified only in rare cases under s. 515(10)(c).
This rarity is consequence of applying s. 515(10)(c), not a precondition or criterion.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues detention justified only in rare cases; court finds rarity is consequence, not precondition, of s. 515(10)(c).

propositions.text: Hall states bail denial ground may be infrequent but essential when it arises.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Hall that bail denial ground may be rare but essential when applicable.

propositions.text: A 'rareness' criterion would be vague, unmanageable, and require improper comparative analysis.
Comparative approach could undermine public confidence in justice administration.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds 'rareness' criterion vague, unmanageable, and potentially undermining public confidence.

propositions.text: s. 515(10)(c) is clear and does not require exceptional or rare circumstances.
Interpretation aligns with Summers decision on sentencing provisions and absence of limiting language on 'circumstances'.
Summers decision interprets 'circumstances' broadly without limitation to exceptional cases.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues s. 515(10)(c) does not require rare circumstances; court agrees citing Summers decision's broad interpretation.

propositions.text: Application of s. 515(10)(c) is not limited to exceptional, unexplainable crimes, or murder only.
Crown can rely on s. 515(10)(c) for any crime but must prove detention justified to maintain confidence in justice.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes s. 515(10)(c) applies broadly; Crown must prove detention justified to maintain confidence in justice.

propositions.text: Section 515(10)(c) lists four circumstances to consider in detention decision, requiring balancing their combined effect.

paragraphs.summary: Court states s. 515(10)(c) requires considering four factors in balance to decide on detention.

propositions.text: Accused presumed innocent at this stage regardless of offence gravity or prosecution strength.

paragraphs.summary: Court reminds accused is presumed innocent regardless of offence gravity or prosecution strength at this stage.

propositions.text: Interim release hearing is summary with flexible evidence rules; some evidence may be excluded at trial.
Justice may find prosecution case unrealistically strong due to hearing's expeditious nature.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes interim release hearing is summary with flexible evidence; justice may overestimate prosecution strength.

propositions.text: Justice must determine apparent strength of prosecution's case without acting as trial judge or jury.
Justice must consider quality and weight of prosecution evidence in balancing exercise.

paragraphs.summary: Court states justice must assess prosecution's apparent case strength carefully without trial role, considering evidence quality.

propositions.text: Justice must consider any defence raised by accused in assessing prosecution's apparent case strength.
Quebec Court of Appeal held justice must consider prosecution weaknesses and defences at release hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Court states justice must consider accused's defence and prosecution weaknesses per Quebec Court of Appeal at release hearing.

propositions.text: Justice must determine objective gravity of offence based on Criminal Code maximum and minimum sentences.

paragraphs.summary: Court states justice must assess offence gravity objectively by Criminal Code sentencing provisions.

propositions.text: Lists possible circumstances relevant under s. 515(10)(c) including violent offences, domestic violence, gang involvement, vulnerable victims, and extent of accused's participation
Aggravating or mitigating factors considered for sentencing can also be relevant under s. 515(10)(c)

paragraphs.summary: The court lists circumstances relevant under s. 515(10)(c), including violent offences, vulnerable victims, and sentencing factors.

propositions.text: The fourth circumstance in s. 515(10)(c) is the accused's liability for a potentially lengthy imprisonment or minimum three years for firearm offences

paragraphs.summary: The court states the fourth circumstance in s. 515(10)(c) involves potential lengthy imprisonment or minimum three years for firearm offences.

propositions.text: Whether a strict rule should be established for what constitutes a 'lengthy term of imprisonment' under s. 515(10)(c)
Some guidance is required for justices to assess 'lengthy term of imprisonment' under s. 515(10)(c)

paragraphs.summary: The court considers if a strict rule for 'lengthy term of imprisonment' is needed and concludes some guidance is required.

propositions.text: No crime is exempt from s. 515(10)(c), so 'lengthy term of imprisonment' does not only mean life sentence

paragraphs.summary: The court finds 'lengthy term of imprisonment' under s. 515(10)(c) is not limited to life sentences.

propositions.text: Justice must consider all case circumstances and sentencing principles known at hearing to determine liability for 'lengthy term of imprisonment'
Justice must avoid complex sentence calculations and not substitute for trial judge
Mitigating or aggravating circumstances with merit may be considered subjectively for 'lengthy term of imprisonment'
This fourth circumstance is assessed subjectively, unlike the second circumstance which is assessed objectively

paragraphs.summary: The court explains justices must consider case circumstances subjectively for 'lengthy term of imprisonment' without complex sentencing calculations.

propositions.text: Appellant argues detention must be ordered if four s. 515(10)(c) circumstances favor it, unless other circumstances justify release

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues detention is mandatory if four s. 515(10)(c) circumstances favor it unless other circumstances justify release.

propositions.text: The appellant's argument is mistaken

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the appellant's argument as mistaken.

propositions.text: Section 515(10)(c) refers to 'all the circumstances, including...' so detention is not automatic when four circumstances favor it
Parliament intended a balancing exercise focusing on specified factors, not automatic detention
Chief Justice in Hall stated detention requires considering all relevant circumstances and maintaining public confidence
Detention only if reasonable community member would be satisfied denial is necessary to maintain confidence in justice

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 515(10)(c) requires balancing all circumstances; detention is not automatic even if four factors favor it.

propositions.text: Test under s. 515(10)(c) is whether detention is necessary to maintain confidence in administration of justice
Four listed circumstances are main factors to balance with others to determine necessity of detention
Automatic detention if four circumstances favor it conflicts with required balancing and purpose of s. 515(10)(c)

paragraphs.summary: The court states detention must be necessary to maintain public confidence, balancing all factors; automatic detention is incompatible.

propositions.text: Release of accused is the cardinal rule; detention is the exception under Canadian law
Morales confirms release is default; detention requires just cause under s. 11(e) Charter
Presumption of innocence under s. 11(d) Charter requires detention be truly justified

paragraphs.summary: The court emphasizes release is default; detention requires just cause and must respect presumption of innocence under Charter.

propositions.text: Personal circumstances of accused and impact on victim and society may be relevant under s. 515(10)(c)
Trial delay may also be considered by justice

paragraphs.summary: The court notes personal circumstances, victim status, societal impact, and trial delay may be relevant under s. 515(10)(c).

propositions.text: French version of s. 515(10)(c) uses 'public confidence' though English version omits 'public'
Court confirmed detention under s. 515(10)(c) is based on maintaining public confidence in justice
Justice's balancing must be guided by perspective of the 'public'

paragraphs.summary: The court explains detention under s. 515(10)(c) is to maintain public confidence, guiding justice's balancing of circumstances.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal in Mordue distinguished 'public confidence' from 'public safety' under s. 515(10)(c) and (b)
Public confidence includes broader concerns than public safety and must be considered separately
Bail judge erred by focusing on bail arrangements and not considering public confidence effect of release

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Mordue that public confidence is broader than public safety and must be separately considered in bail decisions.

propositions.text: Hall explained 'public' means reasonable community members informed about law, Charter values, and case circumstances

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Hall defining 'public' as reasonable, informed community members.

propositions.text: Quebec Court of Appeal in Lamothe explained public often has negative emotional attitudes towards criminals
Public perception must be reasonable and informed, not emotional or lowest common denominator
Judges must not base interim release decisions on visceral public attitudes

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Lamothe that public perception must be reasonable and informed, not emotional, in interim release decisions.

propositions.text: The court finds Lamothe's comments remain relevant

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Lamothe's comments on public perception remain relevant.

propositions.text: 'Public' in s. 515(10)(c) means reasonable, well-informed persons, not legal experts or emotional members
Public confidence cannot be equated with legal experts' confidence in justice administration
Parliament's use of 'public' requires giving meaning to this choice in detention decisions

paragraphs.summary: The court explains 'public' means reasonable, informed persons, not legal experts, and this meaning must guide detention decisions.

propositions.text: R. v. Collins defines reasonable person as dispassionate, fully apprised, reflecting community values
Reasonable person test reminds judges to ground discretion in long-term community values, not passion or stress

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Collins defining reasonable person as dispassionate and grounded in community values for judicial discretion.

propositions.text: Reasonable public member knows rule of law, Charter values, presumption of innocence, right to liberty, and trial within reasonable time
Reasonable public member understands mens rea and defences like mental disorder but not all legal subtleties
Public member expects serious crimes with overwhelming evidence and admission of guilt to be treated accordingly

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the reasonable public member's knowledge of law, rights, defences, and expectations about serious crimes.

propositions.text: Person in s. 515(10)(c) is thoughtful, not emotional, and reasonably informed but not a legal expert

paragraphs.summary: The court states the person in s. 515(10)(c) is thoughtful, reasonably informed, but not a legal expert.

propositions.text: Judges must balance unrealistic public expectations and the need to resist emotional public reactions.
This balancing is difficult in the era of diversified information sources and social media.

paragraphs.summary: The court states judges must balance unrealistic public expectations and resist emotional reactions, especially given modern information sources and social media.

propositions.text: Canadians may think they are well informed but often are not.
Social media enable quick, wide, and effective public reactions, causing chain reactions.
Courts must avoid yielding to emotional or inadequately informed public reactions.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Canadians may be poorly informed and social media amplify reactions, so courts must avoid emotional or uninformed public influence.

propositions.text: Courts must be sensitive to reasonable, well-informed public perceptions to maintain confidence and prevent mob justice.
Quebec Court of Appeal in R. v. Turcotte found media reports are risky as proof due to inaccuracies and lack of legal principles.
Most media reports do not satisfy the reasonable person test for release decisions.

paragraphs.summary: The court says courts must consider reasonable public perceptions; Quebec Court of Appeal found media reports unreliable and not meeting reasonable person standards.

propositions.text: Courts should not automatically disregard media evidence as media reflect some public opinions.
In Canadian Broadcasting Corp v. New Brunswick, media play a vital role in democratic society by informing the public.
Media opinion evidence is admissible and relevant if it corresponds to the reasonable person's opinion.

paragraphs.summary: The court states media evidence is not automatically disregarded; media inform public and their opinions can be admissible if relevant to reasonable person views.

propositions.text: Turcotte has not been reviewed by this Court, so the Court will not comment on its correctness.
The soundness of Turcotte's conclusion must be assessed in light of principles outlined here.

paragraphs.summary: The court will not comment on Turcotte's correctness but says its soundness must be assessed against principles outlined here.

propositions.text: Public confidence in justice can be undermined by unjustified detention or unjustified refusal to detain.

paragraphs.summary: The court states public confidence is undermined by both unjustified detention and unjustified refusal to detain.

propositions.text: Section 515(10)(c) Cr. C. is a distinct ground for pre-trial detention, not residual to (a) and (b).
Section 515(10)(c) must not be interpreted narrowly or applied only in rare cases or certain crimes.
The four circumstances in s. 515(10)(c) are not exhaustive.
Detention must not be automatic even if the four circumstances support it.
All case circumstances must be considered, with attention to the four listed.
Whether a crime is 'unexplainable' or 'unexplained' is not a guiding criterion.
No single circumstance is determinative; combined effect must be considered.
The ultimate question is whether detention is necessary to maintain public confidence in justice.
The court must adopt the perspective of a reasonable, informed public person, not a legal expert.
Public confidence is undermined by unjustified detention or unjustified refusal to detain.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes s. 515(10)(c) principles: it is a distinct, broad ground; all circumstances considered; detention justified if needed to maintain reasonable public confidence.

propositions.text: Serious or violent crimes, overwhelming evidence, and vulnerable victims usually justify pre-trial detention.

paragraphs.summary: The court states serious crimes, strong evidence, and vulnerable victims usually lead to pre-trial detention.

propositions.text: After interpreting s. 515(10)(c), the Court will consider superior court judges' power to review release or detention orders under ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court will now consider superior court judges' review powers under ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. after interpreting s. 515(10)(c).

propositions.text: Section 520 allows accused to apply for review of interim detention orders by a justice.
Section 521 allows prosecutor to apply for review of release orders.
Applications under ss. 520 and 521 may be made anytime before trial.
These sections apply only to offences other than those in s. 469 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains ss. 520 and 521 allow accused or prosecutor to apply for review of detention or release orders before trial, excluding s. 469 offences.

propositions.text: This Court is considering for the first time the scope of ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. review process.
Lower courts disagree on whether the review is an appeal, a de novo hearing, or a hybrid remedy.
Some courts require error of law for review; others allow full discretion; others allow new evidence and error of law claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes this is the first time it considers ss. 520 and 521 scope; lower courts disagree on review nature: appeal, de novo, or hybrid.

propositions.text: Ss. 520 and 521 do not give open-ended discretion to vary initial detention or release decisions.
Ss. 520 and 521 establish a hybrid remedy with greater scope than an appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes ss. 520 and 521 do not allow open-ended discretion but provide a hybrid remedy broader than an appeal.

propositions.text: Ss. 520(1) and (7) and 521(1) and (8) establish the power of review.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes ss. 520(1),(7) and 521(1),(8) establish the power of review.

propositions.text: Ss. 520 and 521 do not provide for a de novo hearing, unlike Youth Criminal Justice Act s. 33(1).
If Parliament intended de novo hearings under ss. 520 and 521, it would have specified this.
Ss. 520(7) and 521(8) require review based on transcript and exhibits, though some new evidence is admissible.
These factors confirm ss. 520 and 521 do not establish a de novo proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds ss. 520 and 521 do not provide de novo hearings, as Parliament did not specify and review is based on transcripts with limited new evidence.

propositions.text: Ss. 520 and 521 limit review to cases where cause is shown, unlike broader discretion in Young Offenders Act s. 16(9),(10).
This Court found 'discretion' wording in Young Offenders Act conferred broad review power.
Parliament did not use 'discretion' wording in ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes ss. 520 and 521 require cause to show for review, unlike broader discretion under Young Offenders Act, which used 'discretion' wording.

propositions.text: Wording of ss. 520 and 521 precludes open-ended discretion for reviewing judge.
This conclusion will be tested by comparison with similar provisions and nature of initial release decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes ss. 520 and 521 wording precludes open-ended discretion, to be confirmed by comparison with similar provisions.

propositions.text: Difference in wording between ss. 520(7)(e), 521(8)(e) and s. 680(1) Cr. C. supports greater deference to initial release decision.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues wording differences between ss. 520(7)(e), 521(8)(e) and s. 680(1) Cr. C. favor more deference to initial release decisions.

propositions.text: Section 680(1) Cr. C. deals with review of release decisions for offences in s. 469 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 680(1) Cr. C. governs review of release decisions for s. 469 offences.

propositions.text: Appellant concedes case law on s. 680 Cr. C. review nature is inconsistent.
Provincial courts of appeal recognize inconsistency in s. 680 Cr. C. review case law.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant concedes and provincial courts recognize inconsistency in case law on s. 680 Cr. C. review nature.

propositions.text: Section 18(2) Extradition Act allows court of appeal judge to review judicial interim release decisions and confirm, vary, or substitute decisions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 18(2) Extradition Act allows court of appeal judge to review and vary judicial interim release decisions.

propositions.text: Decisions available to reviewing judge resemble those in s. 520 Cr. C.
Unlike s. 680(1) Cr. C., s. 18(2) Extradition Act does not limit variation to cases where 'cause' is shown.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds reviewing judge's decisions resemble s. 520 Cr. C., but s. 18(2) Extradition Act lacks 'cause' limitation unlike s. 680(1) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Canadian appellate courts nearly unanimously hold s. 18(2) Extradition Act allows review only for error in principle.
Cites multiple appellate cases supporting error in principle standard under s. 18(2) Extradition Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Canadian appellate courts nearly unanimously require error in principle for review under s. 18(2) Extradition Act, citing cases.

propositions.text: Only BC Court of Appeal holds review must determine if initial decision is 'correct' while deferring to first judge's fact findings.
Cites BC Court of Appeal cases Seifert and Graham supporting this position.
BC and NL Courts of Appeal reached different outcomes despite both analogizing to s. 680 Cr. C. review procedure.
Disagreement among courts on nature of s. 680 Cr. C. review procedure explains differing outcomes.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds only BC Court of Appeal requires 'correct' decision standard with deference; BC and NL courts differ on s. 680 Cr. C. review nature.

propositions.text: No need to decide validity of appellate positions on s. 680(1) Cr. C. and s. 18(2) Extradition Act for this appeal.
Comparison of s. 680(1) Cr. C. and s. 18(2) Extradition Act with ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. is relevant.
Unlike ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C., s. 680(1) Cr. C. and s. 18(2) Extradition Act do not require cause to be shown for review.
Parliament intended ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. to limit reviewing judge's discretion.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no need to decide appellate positions but notes ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. limit discretion unlike s. 680(1) Cr. C. and s. 18(2) Extradition Act.

propositions.text: Appellant argues interim release decision should be reviewed like sentencing appeals under s. 687 Cr. C.
Appellant relies on multiple Supreme Court cases to support error in principle or clear unreasonableness standard for review under ss. 520 and 521.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues interim release decisions should be reviewed like sentencing appeals, citing Supreme Court cases for error in principle or unreasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Respondent argues distinctions between sentencing and interim release decisions are too great to equate their review rules.
Respondent asserts interim release is a constitutional right, unlike sentencing principle on less restrictive sanctions.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the differences between sentencing and interim release decisions prevent equating their review rules, emphasizing constitutional right to interim release.

propositions.text: There are similarities between interim release and sentencing decisions: both discretionary with specific statutory rules.
Both have relaxed evidence rules: ss. 518 and 723 Cr. C.
Release must be ordered unless prosecution shows cause under s. 515(2) and (10) Cr. C.
Sentencing judge must choose least restrictive sanction per s. 718.2(d) Cr. C.
Judge's options for interim release include release without conditions, conditions, deposit, or detention under s. 515.
Sentencing options include discharge, probation, fine, or imprisonment under ss. 730, 731, 734, 732.1(3) Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds similarities between interim release and sentencing decisions, including discretion, relaxed evidence rules, and statutory options for release or sentence.

propositions.text: Significant differences exist between interim release and sentencing decisions.
Toronto Star Newspapers Ltd. v. Canada explains expeditious nature of interim release system and its implications.
Interim release hearing must occur within 24 hours; prosecution has limited time to gather evidence.
Adjournment of bail hearing limited to three days without accused's consent; orders can be reviewed with notice.
Prosecution may lead any credible or trustworthy evidence, including untested or hearsay evidence under s. 518(1)(e).
Justice has broad discretion to inquire of accused; process is informal and can be by phone.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds significant differences in interim release's expeditious, informal process with broad evidence admissibility compared to sentencing.

propositions.text: Expedited release hearing reflects importance of presumption of innocence and individual liberty.
Accused often has little time to choose counsel or prepare defense at release hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds expedited release hearings protect presumption of innocence but limit accused's preparation time and counsel access.

propositions.text: Sentencing judge often presided over trial and has analyzed abundant evidence, unlike release justice.
Sentencing judge is more familiar with accused's situation than release justice.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds sentencing judges have more evidence and familiarity with accused than release justices.

propositions.text: At sentencing, accused is convicted and no longer presumed innocent.
Sentencing may have longer-term impact than interim detention.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds accused is no longer presumed innocent at sentencing, which may have longer-term impact than interim detention.

propositions.text: Comparison between interim release and sentencing decisions is interesting but not determinative due to differences.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes comparison between interim release and sentencing decisions is interesting but not determinative due to differences.

propositions.text: Interim release decision is often called 'discretionary' but release remains the rule unless detention justified under s. 515(10) Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds interim release decisions are discretionary but release is the default unless detention is justified.

propositions.text: Justice must balance factors under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C. involving fact findings and weight assessment.
This balancing makes the decision appropriately characterized as discretionary.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the justice's balancing of factors under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C. makes the release decision discretionary.

propositions.text: Sentencing decisions are discretionary and courts interfere only if sentence is clearly excessive or inadequate.
Cites Shropshire and Muise for sentencing appeal principles emphasizing acceptable range and discretion.
Sentencing is an exercise of judgment considering legal principles and circumstances, not an exact science.
Courts of Appeal review sentences only if outside acceptable range or error in principle.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds sentencing decisions are discretionary, reviewed only if clearly excessive, inadequate, or erroneous in principle, citing Shropshire and Muise.

propositions.text: Nasogaluak states appellate courts should not interfere with sentencing for mere difference in weighing factors.
Only unreasonable exercise of discretion by trial judge justifies appellate interference on error in principle grounds.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Nasogaluak that appellate courts interfere only if sentencing discretion is unreasonably exercised, not for different factor weighting.

propositions.text: Accused presumed innocent at release hearing but not at sentencing.
Release decisions involve balancing difficult factors, a delicate exercise.
Open-ended discretion for reviewing judge to substitute assessment would distort essence of release decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds release decisions require delicate balancing and open-ended review discretion would distort their essence.

propositions.text: Ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. do not provide for de novo hearing.
Without new evidence, reviewing judge is not better positioned than justice to assess detention necessity.
Reviewing judge has no special expertise over justice regarding release decisions.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. do not allow de novo review; reviewing judge lacks better position or expertise than justice.

propositions.text: No justification exists for reviewing judge to always substitute their assessment for justice's in release decisions.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes no justification exists for reviewing judge to always substitute their assessment for justice's in release decisions.

propositions.text: Ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. do not grant open-ended review power over initial detention or release orders.
Reviewing judge must determine appropriateness of exercising review power under these sections.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. limit review power and reviewing judge must decide if review is appropriate.

propositions.text: Intervention appropriate if justice erred in law or decision was clearly inappropriate by misweighting factors.
Reviewing judge cannot interfere simply for different weighing of factors.
Relevant factors not limited to those in s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.
Reviewing judge may vary decision if new evidence shows material, relevant change under ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states intervention is proper for legal error, clear inappropriateness, or new evidence showing material change under ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Sections 520(7) and 521(8) Cr. C. allow tendering of new evidence or exhibits.
Section 520(7) text is provided.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes ss. 520(7) and 521(8) Cr. C. permit new evidence or exhibits, quoting s. 520(7).

propositions.text: What qualifies as admissible new evidence?

paragraphs.summary: The court poses the issue of what constitutes admissible new evidence.

propositions.text: New evidence limited to facts truly new since initial decision, excluding facts available earlier to prevent judge shopping.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues new evidence must be truly new, excluding facts available earlier to avoid judge shopping.

propositions.text: Appellant fears judge shopping if old evidence admitted on review.
Finality and avoiding multiple proceedings are important to prevent judge shopping.
Appellant's argument goes too far; detained persons seek release quickly and do not withhold evidence.
Cites Toronto Star Newspapers Ltd., Hall, and Ell v. Alberta on impact of detention on individuals.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's judge shopping fear exaggerated, citing case law and noting detainees seek quick release.

propositions.text: Further review applications require leave and 30-day wait under ss. 520(8) and 521(9) Cr. C.
This limits risk of judge shopping and supports rejecting appellant's fear.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes leave and 30-day wait limit further reviews, reducing judge shopping risk, rejecting appellant's fear.

propositions.text: Detained persons may not tender all evidence initially due to expeditious process, lack of representation, incomplete evidence.
Courts should adopt a broad view of admissible new evidence under ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. to serve justice.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds initial evidence may be incomplete due to process and urges broad view of new evidence admissibility.

propositions.text: Palmer criteria for new evidence on appeal: due diligence, relevance, credibility, potential effect on result.
Palmer criteria reproduced in R. v. Warsing, para. 50.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Palmer criteria for new evidence: due diligence, relevance, credibility, and effect on result.

propositions.text: Palmer criteria relevant with modifications for ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. reviews due to expeditious nature and rights risks.
Rules of evidence relaxed at release hearing per s. 518 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Palmer criteria apply with flexibility and relaxed evidence rules under s. 518 Cr. C. for reviews.

propositions.text: Due diligence ensures finality and order essential to criminal process integrity.
Appellant relies on finality and order to limit new evidence.
Pre-trial detention is often interim, not final, affecting due diligence application.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains due diligence ensures finality, appellant relies on it, but detention's interim nature affects its strictness.

propositions.text: Due diligence less strict in criminal than civil cases (Palmer, McMartin).
Weight of due diligence depends on totality of circumstances (Price, Warsing).
Appellate court should determine why evidence was unavailable at trial (G.D.B.).
Generous interpretation of new evidence consistent with Court principles.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites authorities that due diligence is flexible and generous interpretation of new evidence is consistent with principles.

propositions.text: Reviewing judge may consider truly new evidence or pre-existing evidence not tendered for legitimate reasons.
Due diligence criterion from Palmer must be understood flexibly in ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. context.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes reviewing judges may admit new or pre-existing evidence not tendered for legitimate reasons, applying due diligence flexibly.

propositions.text: New evidence not limited to that unavailable before initial hearing, e.g., late prosecutor disclosure.
Reviewing judge must determine if accused's failure to tender evidence earlier was legitimate and reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds new evidence includes late-disclosed evidence and reviewing judge must assess legitimacy of prior non-tendering.

propositions.text: Reviewing judge may refuse evidence if accused sought to delay or engage in judge shopping.
New evidence conception balances criminal justice integrity and accused rights in expeditious proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: The court states judges may refuse evidence if abused and that new evidence rules balance justice system integrity and accused rights.

propositions.text: Second Palmer criterion relaxed: evidence must be relevant for s. 515(10) Cr. C., not necessarily decisive.
Justice must consider all circumstances under s. 515(10)(c).
Second criterion rarely decisive in ss. 520 and 521 Cr. C. reviews due to broad relevance.

paragraphs.summary: The court relaxes second Palmer criterion to broad relevance under s. 515(10)(c), rarely decisive in reviews.

propositions.text: Third Palmer criterion (credibility) interpreted with relaxed evidence rules at bail stage per s. 518(1)(e) Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court interprets credibility criterion with relaxed bail evidence rules under s. 518(1)(e) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Fourth Palmer criterion modified: new evidence must reasonably affect balancing under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.
New evidence must be significant to affect detention justification.

paragraphs.summary: The court modifies fourth Palmer criterion requiring new evidence to significantly affect s. 515(10)(c) balancing.

propositions.text: If new evidence admissible, reviewing judge repeats s. 515(10)(c) analysis as initial decision-maker.
Reviewing judge must consider all circumstances and balance public perspective on detention.
Palmer criteria serve as flexible guidelines, not procedural constraints delaying release process.
Release process requires expeditious, flexible procedure.

paragraphs.summary: The court directs reviewing judges to reanalyze under s. 515(10)(c) using Palmer criteria flexibly without delaying release.

propositions.text: Reviewing judge can intervene with relevant new evidence, legal error, or clearly inappropriate decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes intervention is allowed for relevant new evidence, legal error, or clearly inappropriate decisions.

propositions.text: Judge Lavergne considered witnesses' testimony of respondent and co-accused abusing and threatening bus driver.
Judge noted video showed spitting at driver provoking his reaction and assault initiation.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found respondent and co-accused abused and threatened driver, provoking assault per witnesses and video.

propositions.text: Martin J. found not all incident elements were before Judge Lavergne, who started events when three men stood up on bus
Martin J. said events started when driver refused to open bus doors at previous stop
Driver jumped up after men got off, had verbal exchange, then sat down followed by men who reboarded
Driver took physical action against one individual, after which situation degenerated

paragraphs.summary: Martin J. found Judge Lavergne lacked full incident evidence, noting earlier bus door refusal, driver’s physical action, and event sequence.

propositions.text: Judge Lavergne did not state driver refused boarding at previous stop
Transcript suggests counsel did not discuss bus door refusal
Judge Lavergne did not mention driver’s physical action before assault
Passenger statement with these details was given to respondent’s counsel only morning of hearing
Investigating officer referenced passenger statement but did not mention physical action
Respondent’s counsel did not cross-examine officer on passenger statement
Late receipt of passenger statement justified not using it at initial hearing but using it later

paragraphs.summary: Court found Judge Lavergne lacked some evidence; passenger statement was late and not used initially but reasonably used later.

propositions.text: At second release hearing, respondent’s counsel said bus driver did not stop at previous stop
Counsel said driver spoke aggressively and pushed young men after being spat at
Counsel filed passenger’s statement in evidence at second hearing

paragraphs.summary: At second hearing, respondent’s counsel argued driver did not stop earlier, alleged driver’s aggression, and filed passenger statement.

propositions.text: Judge Legault noted young men complained driver did not wait at previous stop
Judge Legault observed young men threw pizza and spat at driver, who objected at bus door

paragraphs.summary: Judge Legault found young men complained about driver’s prior stop and that driver objected after being spat at.

propositions.text: Judge Legault found detention justified under s. 515(10)(c) Cr. C.
Judge Legault agreed with Judge Lavergne’s observations on confidence in justice administration
Factors included likelihood of conviction, offence gravity, lack of independence prospects, and potential lengthy imprisonment
Judge Legault saw no evidence to alter findings on aggravating factors and accused’s significant participation

paragraphs.summary: Judge Legault upheld detention citing conviction likelihood, offence gravity, and aggravating factors, agreeing with Judge Lavergne.

propositions.text: No new facts were presented to Martin J. on review
Judge Legault had all incident elements at preliminary inquiry and found new details did not alter Judge Lavergne’s conclusion

paragraphs.summary: Court found no new facts for Martin J.; Judge Legault had full evidence and upheld Judge Lavergne’s conclusion.

propositions.text: Judge Legault did not mention driver’s physical action but was aware and considered it
Judge need not show knowledge of law or all evidence aspects: R. v. Burns
Judge did not fail to appreciate or disregard relevant evidence: Harper v. The Queen
Driver’s physical action alone could not tip balance in respondent’s favour

paragraphs.summary: Court found Judge Legault considered driver’s physical action; cited case law on judge’s duty and concluded action insufficient to favor respondent.

propositions.text: Martin J. could not review initial detention order based on new facts

paragraphs.summary: Court concluded Martin J. lacked basis to review detention order on new facts.

propositions.text: Judge Lavergne properly identified s. 515(10)(c) test as whether release denial maintains public confidence

paragraphs.summary: Judge Lavergne correctly stated s. 515(10)(c) test about denying release to maintain public confidence.

propositions.text: Judge Lavergne said public means reasonable, informed persons aware of legislative values and crime circumstances
Judge Lavergne said prosecutor bears onus to justify detention
Judge Lavergne’s statement consistent with this Court’s decision in Hall

paragraphs.summary: Judge Lavergne defined public as reasonable informed persons and placed onus on prosecutor, consistent with Hall decision.

propositions.text: Judge Lavergne did not elaborate on prosecution’s burden under s. 515(10)(c)
Overall decision detailed enough for review to understand detention grounds
Judge Lavergne referred to first three factors and noted accused liable for significant term
Under s. 515(10)(b), Judge Lavergne considered abuse, spitting, driver’s likely words, and assault
Judge Lavergne noted respondent’s active participation and high conviction likelihood due to videotape

paragraphs.summary: Court found Judge Lavergne’s decision sufficiently detailed, considering factors and strong prosecution evidence including videotape.

propositions.text: Judge Lavergne stressed assault’s brutality, gratuitousness, and unexplainable nature
Assault was incomprehensible as defendant and driver were strangers with no predisposition
Unpredictable conduct weighs against release

paragraphs.summary: Judge Lavergne emphasized assault’s brutality, senselessness, and that such conduct disfavors release.

propositions.text: Judge Lavergne’s reasons suggest unexplainable assault influenced detention under s. 515(10)(c)
Whether offence is unexplainable is not a criterion under s. 515(10)(c)

paragraphs.summary: Court found unexplainable offence influenced Judge Lavergne but is not a s. 515(10)(c) criterion.

propositions.text: Martin J. made crime being explainable a criterion and unduly restricted s. 515(10)(c) scope
Martin J. found incident was not totally gratuitous or unexplainable
Martin J. reviewed s. 515(10) history and case law, finding s. 515(10)(c) to be used sparingly

paragraphs.summary: Martin J. used explainability as criterion, found incident not totally unexplainable, and said s. 515(10)(c) used sparingly.

propositions.text: Martin J. disagreed incident was unexplainable but acknowledged heinous behaviour

paragraphs.summary: Martin J. said behaviour was heinous but not unexplainable.

propositions.text: Martin J. quoted Manitoba Court of Appeal in Trout comparing case facts to Hall

paragraphs.summary: Martin J. cited Trout case comparing brutality to Hall case.

propositions.text: Martin J. erred by narrowly interpreting s. 515(10)(c) and making explainability determinative
Martin J. recognized offence seriousness but reversed lower judges without considering four s. 515(10)(c) factors
Martin J. made errors justifying review of entire decision

paragraphs.summary: Court found Martin J. erred by narrow s. 515(10)(c) view, ignoring factors, and reversing judges, warranting review.

propositions.text: Martin J. intervened without basis as no material change, error of law, or clear inappropriateness existed
Detention of respondent justified under s. 515(10)(c)

paragraphs.summary: Court found Martin J. lacked basis to intervene and that detention was justified under s. 515(10)(c).

propositions.text: All relevant factors must be balanced to determine if detention is necessary to maintain public confidence

paragraphs.summary: Court states all factors must be balanced to decide if detention is necessary for public confidence.

propositions.text: Prosecution’s case is strong due to videotape and eyewitnesses
Videotape is more reliable than circumstantial or testimonial evidence
Respondent appears not to have valid defence even considering driver’s physical action
Respondent did not argue valid defence in this Court
At this stage, evidence does not support self-defence or reasonable force argument under s. 34 Cr. C.
Defence of provocation not available as it only reduces murder charge under s. 232 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds strong prosecution case, no valid defence argued, and self-defence or provocation defences unavailable.

propositions.text: The offence is objectively very serious as it is aggravated assault with a maximum sentence of 14 years, one of the most severe in the Criminal Code after life imprisonment

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the offence is very serious aggravated assault with a maximum 14-year sentence, among the most severe after life imprisonment.

propositions.text: The respondent was an active participant in an extremely brutal assault that passengers could not quickly stop
Violent, brutal or heinous nature of an offence is an important factor for a justice to consider
The driver's refusal to wait at a previous stop is irrelevant to the analysis
The driver's alleged pushing of a friend does not favor the respondent given insults and threats during the ride

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent actively participated in a brutal assault; violent nature is important; driver's prior refusal irrelevant; pushing does not favor respondent.

propositions.text: Maximum sentence for aggravated assault is 14 years; for assault causing bodily harm, 10 years; neither has minimum sentence
Aggravated assault generally demands unconditional imprisonment to express denunciation and deterrence (R. v. Dagenais and others)
Respondent, though young and with no record, likely faces significant imprisonment due to offence circumstances and active participation
Respondent is liable for potentially lengthy imprisonment under s. 515(10)(c) if convicted of aggravated assault or assault causing bodily harm

paragraphs.summary: The court states aggravated assault max 14 years, needs imprisonment for denunciation; respondent likely faces significant term if convicted.

propositions.text: The four circumstances in s. 515(10)(c) strongly support detention of the respondent

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 515(10)(c) circumstances strongly support respondent's detention.

propositions.text: Assault against a bus driver, a civil servant, makes the offence more heinous
Nature, severity, long-term effects, and impact on driver's career and personal life are relevant

paragraphs.summary: The court finds assault on bus driver more heinous; injury nature, severity, and long-term impact are relevant.

propositions.text: Considering all relevant circumstances under s. 515(10)(c), detention of respondent was necessary to maintain confidence in justice

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes detention was necessary to maintain confidence in justice under s. 515(10)(c).

propositions.text: A reasonable, informed public member would not understand why respondent should not remain in custody pending trial
Such public members are not guided by emotions or mob influence but by facts and law
Brutal attack on bus driver with serious health consequences and video evidence shows respondent's active participation
Confidence in justice would be undermined if respondent's interim detention were not ordered

paragraphs.summary: The court finds reasonable public would support custody; brutal attack and video evidence justify detention to maintain confidence.

propositions.text: Appeal is allowed; Superior Court judge erred by interfering with initial release decision and restricting s. 515(10)(c) scope
Detention of respondent is justified under s. 515(10)(c) and detention order is restored

paragraphs.summary: The court allows appeal, finds Superior Court erred, and restores detention order under s. 515(10)(c).
